elements.evidence: Section 9.4 expressly permits Customer to terminate the Agreement or any Order Form for convenience.
Section 9.4 requires prior written notice to Vendor.
Section 9.4 specifies thirty days' prior notice.

elements.element: Vendor must refund prepaid fees upon Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Section 9.4 requires Vendor to refund prepaid Fees following the termination.

elements.element: The refund must be pro-rated to the prepaid period after the effective date of termination.
elements.evidence: The required refund covers prepaid Fees for the period after the effective date, which implements a pro-rata refund of unused prepaid Fees.

elements.element: Vendor has no termination-for-convenience right during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Section 9.4 expressly states that Vendor has no right to terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience during a term.
Section 9.4 expressly grants Customer a termination-for-convenience right.
The clause requires only 30 days' notice, which is outside the specified 60–90-day range.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee must not exceed three months' fees.
elements.evidence: The clause expressly prohibits any penalty or early-termination charge, so no fee exceeding the cap can apply.
The clause does not grant Vendor an affirmative termination-for-convenience right and instead prohibits such termination during a term.

elements.element: Vendor's convenience termination may take effect only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: The express prohibition on Vendor termination for convenience during a term imposes at least the required restriction against an earlier effective date, although no affirmative end-of-term right is granted.

elements.element: Vendor must provide 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: No 90-day Vendor notice requirement appears in the operative language.

result.reason: The operative redline fully implements the preferred position. The fallback is not independently satisfied because Customer notice is 30 rather than 60–90 days, and Vendor receives neither an affirmative end-of-term convenience-termination right nor a 90-day notice mechanism. The redline preserves the existing cause-based termination rights and introduces no direct contradiction. It is not strictly minimal because it additionally permits termination in whole or in part and adds a broad waiver of penalty, early-termination charges, and other liability beyond the expressly stated preferred requirements; the phrase “other liability” is also somewhat broader than necessary.
